_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-15) post: '214 saves commits' reads '214 saved versions' (commit is explained in the next paragraph)
title: Secrets in the Walls
setting: a house with notes hidden in the walls

post.author: u/gowrie_restorer_somerled
post.title: I restore old houses at night and keep finding notes the owners thought were gone. Tonight my sister's flower shop got an invoice for 3,200 hours of computing.

blocks.text: I'm Somerled. I restore old houses at night, while the owners sleep somewhere else. This month it's the Murchison house in Gowrie. Behind the plaster I keep finding notes the old owners thought were gone: a rent receipt, a letter someone meant to burn. Nobody ever took them out. They just papered over them.
By day I also built the website for my sister Eirwen's flower shop. Tonight her shop found a note in its own walls.

The site rents its computers from a cloud company: machines in someone else's building, paid by the hour. A program proves it may use the shop's account with a cloud key, a long secret that works like a password. In this post it appears only as KEY-REDACTED.
The site's code lives in a repository, a shared folder that keeps every saved version of every file: its history. Ours holds 214 saved versions over 227 days, since Sunday 1 March.
Ours is also public: anyone online can read it, history included. A private one opens only to people you invite.

Each save is called a commit. On Thursday 19 March at 23:47 I wanted the photo uploads working before bed. I pasted the key into a settings file and saved commit 41. At 00:03 I saw my mistake, deleted the line and saved commit 42, "remove key". Then I typed the key by hand into a file on the rented computer.

That key does more than photos. Our pipeline, the automatic steps that put each new version live, uses it to start the rented computer. One key was easier than two, so I made it from the account's main login, with every right the account has. Starting computers is one of them.

At 22:00 tonight the cloud company emailed Eirwen an invoice. It bills early when a month's computing reaches $4,000. A use record came with it. Each line shows the time, the key, what it did and where the request came from; the last line is the invoice.

Tue 13 Oct 02:00  KEY-REDACTED  start 160 computers     from: not ours
invoice 1 to 13 Oct 2026: 3,200 computer-hours at $1.25 = $4,000.00
Every bill before was a few dollars for storing photos. A shop that sells flowers paid for 3,200 hours of someone else's computing.

blocks.label: repository_and_invoice.png

diagram.aria: My sketch of what happened. Top row: commit 41 on Thursday 19 March 2026 at 23:47 put the key in; commit 42 on Friday 20 March at 00:03 deleted the line; the history, 214 commits and public, still holds commit 41. Bottom row: on Tuesday 13 October at 02:00 the key started 160 computers that are not ours; at 22:00 the invoice came: 3,200 computer-hours, $4,000.00. A note says the key is still valid.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from my sketch. Commit 42 deleted the line on 20 March, but commit 41 is still in the public history of 214 commits. On Tuesday 13 October at 02:00 the key started 160 computers that are not ours, and at 22:00 the invoice came: 3,200 computer-hours at $1.25, $4,000.00. The key still works.

blocks.text: Deleting a line is one more layer of wallpaper. The note is still behind it.

Eirwen rang me straight away. Commit 42 took the key out of the newest version, but anyone can still open commit 41. Programs watch public code for anything shaped like a key and try what they find. It works because a key proves nothing about whose hand holds it. Nobody can say who copied it, or when.
It's 22:30 and the key still works. Every hour adds 160 computer-hours, $200. The cloud's key page has a button to revoke a key: cancel it for good, so it opens nothing ever again.

The cloud company also offers a secrets store, a locked service. When the site starts, it asks the store for its key; the store checks the site may have it, then hands it over. No key ever sits in the code.
What should I change tonight, and in what order?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Notes in the walls. A history works like that wall: a later commit papers over a line, it never takes it out. Before you choose, two questions. Does the key work at this minute? And who might hold a copy of commit 41 that you can never reach? One more word for the thread: secret scanning. The code host, the site that keeps your repository, checks commits for anything shaped like a key and flags it: it raises an alert.

replies.author: u/gowrie_restorer_somerled
replies.text: The key page says active, last used just now. There was no spending alert on the account. The invoice was the first anyone heard of it.

comments.author: u/next_commit_olamide
comments.text: Deleting it in the next commit fixed it; nobody reads old history. People look at the newest version, not commit 41 of 214. If it still bothers you, rewrite the history: rebuild every commit as if that line was never typed, then replace the public copy. Then the key isn't on your page at all.

comments.author: u/gowrie_florist_eirwen
comments.text: Eirwen, his sister. I sell flowers. I don't need to know how it works; I need it to stop. My insurer asked one thing on the phone: can we make the repository private, so only the shop's own people can read its code history?

reply.prompt: It's 22:30, the key still works, and every hour adds $200. What should Somerled do tonight? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Revoke the key now and make a new one, then keep keys in a secrets store, not in code.
options.part2: At 22:30 I pressed revoke, and stopped the 160 computers the key had started; the use record listed every one. Then I made new keys with only the rights each job needs, one for photo uploads and one for the pipeline. Both live in the secrets store. The site and the pipeline ask it for them when they start, and no file holds them. In the sim I chose revoke on the night with the secrets store on and replayed: 3,280 computer-hours, $4,100.00, and the cost per hour drops to $0.00 at 22:30 and stays there to the morning. Commit 41 still holds the old key, but it opens nothing now. Eirwen has written to the cloud company about the bill. I turned on secret scanning as well, for next time.
options.senior: Treat a leaked key as already used. Revoke it first, because only revoking stops the cost, and stop whatever it started. Then replace it, then tidy up. GitHub's own advice on an alert is to rotate the affected credential immediately, and it calls removing secrets from history time-intensive and often unnecessary once the credential is revoked. Then fix the cause: keys in a secrets store, fetched when the program starts, never in code; a separate key for each job and each environment, with only the rights it needs; scanning before and after each commit is sent.

options.text: Rewrite the code history to remove the key, so no copy of it is left on the public site.
options.part2: On Olamide's advice I rewrote the history at 22:30: every commit rebuilt without the key, and the public copy replaced. Commit 41 no longer holds it. But copies made before tonight still do, and the key itself was never cancelled. In the sim I turned the rewrite on and left revoke at never: by 06:00 on Wednesday the bill reads 4,480 computer-hours, $5,600.00, still $200 an hour, and the key is still valid.
options.senior: Rewriting treats the repository as the only copy, and it isn't: anything that was public has been copied. It also treats the line in the code as the problem, when the problem is that the key works. GitHub says removing secrets from history is time-intensive and often unnecessary if you've already revoked the credential. Revoke first; rewrite later, if at all, for tidiness.

options.text: Turn on secret scanning so every commit is checked and any key in one raises an alert.
options.part2: I turned on secret scanning at 22:30. It checked the whole history, flagged commit 41 and raised an alert. Then nothing else happened, because an alert cancels nothing. In the sim I set scanning on from tonight and left revoke at never: commit 41 flagged at 22:30, the key still valid, and by 06:00 4,480 computer-hours, $5,600.00. With revoke set to the first scanner alert, it stops at 3,280. With scanning on from the start, it flags commit 41 on 19 March, and revoking then leaves 0 computer-hours.
options.senior: Secret scanning is real practice and worth turning on: GitHub's scanning checks the entire history, and its push protection can block a key before it reaches the repository. But scanning detects; it doesn't cancel. GitHub's advice when an alert arrives is to rotate the affected credential immediately. Switched on tonight, it finds a key already in strangers' hands. Pair it with revoking, and with a secrets store so there is nothing in the code to find.

options.text: Make the repository private, so only the shop's own people can read its code history.
options.part2: At 22:30 the repository went private, as the insurer asked. Strangers can no longer read the history. But the key in it still works, and whoever copied it already has it. In the sim I set the repository private and left revoke at never: by 06:00, 4,480 computer-hours, $5,600.00, and the key still valid.
options.senior: Private changes who can read the code from now on, not who already did, and it does nothing to the key. A private repository isn't a safe place for keys either. In Uber's 2016 breach, the FTC says, the key was posted to a private GitHub repository, and intruders still used it. Code is read by many people and tools; keys belong in a secrets store.

sim.title: Replay the shop's key, from commit 41 to the morning after the invoice
sim.lede: You're Somerled, replaying seven moments. The figures are given data: the public repository holds 214 commits over 227 days, 1 March to 13 October 2026; commit 41 put the cloud key in at 23:47 on Thursday 19 March 2026, and commit 42 deleted the line at 00:03. On Tuesday 13 October at 02:00 the key started 160 computers that are not the shop's, at $1.25 per computer-hour, $200 an hour. The cloud company billed early at 22:00, when the month's computing reached $4,000. Choose when to revoke the key (never, as found; on the night at 22:30; or at the first scanner alert), whether to rewrite the history, whether to make the repository private, when secret scanning is on (off; from tonight; from the start), and whether any new key goes into a secrets store. Step a moment at a time, or run to 06:00 on Wednesday. The key is the label KEY-REDACTED, never a real key.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to the morning as found: 3,200 computer-hours and $4,000.00 on the invoice at 22:00, and 4,480 and $5,600.00 by 06:00, still $200 an hour. Turn on the rewrite: commit 41 no longer holds the key, and the bill is the same. Make the repository private: the same. Turn scanning on from tonight: commit 41 is flagged at 22:30, and the bill is the same. Now revoke on the night with the secrets store on: 3,280 computer-hours, $4,100.00, and nothing more by morning. Last, set scanning on from the start and revoke at the first alert: 0 computer-hours.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke into the shop's account. A cloud key with every right the account had was saved into commit 41 of a public repository, and deleting the line in commit 42 only covered it over: the history kept it. A stranger's program used it to start 160 computers. The fix is to revoke the key at once and stop what it started, then keep keys in a secrets store, never in code, with a separate key for each job and each environment, and scanning before and after each commit.

steps.title: A commit is kept for ever; a deletion is just a newer note.
steps.text: A repository keeps every commit, in order. When you delete a line, the repository doesn't erase it; it saves a new commit in which the line is gone, and the old commit stays exactly as it was. Anyone who can read the repository can open commit 41 and read the key, and anyone who copied the repository before the deletion keeps the key in their copy for good. That is why history is forever: in a public repository, assume anything ever committed has been read.

steps.title: Why one key could start 160 computers.
steps.text: The key was made from the account's main login, so it had every right the account has. It did two jobs, photo uploads and the pipeline that starts the rented computer, because one key was easier than two. The photo job needed only to put files in storage. Had each job its own key with only the rights it needs, called least privilege, the leaked key could have stored photos and nothing else. The same goes for environments: a test copy of the site gets its own keys, so a leak there can't touch the live shop.

steps.title: The night a key leaks, step by step.
steps.text: First, revoke the key, so it opens nothing. Nothing else stops new use: not deleting the line, not rewriting the history, not making the repository private. Second, stop what the key started; revoking stops new requests, but computers already running keep running, so use the use record to find and stop them. Third, make new keys, each with only the rights its job needs, and put them in the secrets store. Fourth, read the use record for anything else the key touched. Last, and only if you want it tidy, rewrite the history. Then tell the people affected and the cloud company.

steps.title: A secrets store, step by step.
steps.text: First, the cloud gives the rented computer its own identity, so it can prove who it is without any key written in a file. Second, when the site starts, it asks the secrets store for the photo key, proving its identity. Third, the store checks that this computer may have that key, records the request and hands it over. Fourth, the site keeps the key in memory only, never on disk or in code. To replace a key, you change it once in the store; every program gets the new one next time it asks. Each environment, test and live, asks for its own key.

steps.title: Scanning before and after the push.
steps.text: A push is sending your commits from your computer up to the shared repository. Push protection checks commits as they are pushed and blocks one that holds something shaped like a key, before it is ever in the repository. Secret scanning checks the whole history after the fact and raises an alert for anything it finds. Use both. Neither cancels a key that has already leaked: an alert is a smoke alarm, not a fire door, and the first thing to do when it rings is revoke.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for tomorrow. Top row: the website code, with no keys in it; the secrets store, which holds the new keys; the rented computer, which asks the store for its key when it starts. Bottom row: secret scanning and push protection, which check every commit of the code; the cloud key page, where the old key is revoked; the two new keys, one for photos and one for the pipeline, each with only the rights its job needs, kept in the store.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tomorrow. The old key is revoked and its 160 computers stopped. Two new keys, one per job, each with only the rights it needs, live in the secrets store; the rented computer asks for them when it starts, and the code holds none. Scanning checks every commit. Replayed, the bill stops at 3,280 computer-hours, $4,100.00.

fix.title: The fix: revoke first, then keys in a secrets store, one per job, and scanning on every commit
fix.text: Revoke the leaked key tonight and stop the computers it started, using the use record to find them. Make new keys, one for photo uploads and one for the pipeline, each with only the rights its job needs, and a separate set for any test copy of the site. Put them in the cloud company's secrets store; the site and the pipeline ask for them when they start, and no file or commit holds them. Turn on push protection, so a commit holding something shaped like a key is blocked before it reaches the repository, and secret scanning, so anything already there raises an alert. Set a spending alert on the account, so the next surprise is a message within the day rather than an invoice. In the sim, revoking at 22:30 holds the bill at 3,280 computer-hours, $4,100.00. Rewriting the history afterwards is optional tidying, not a fix.

limits: Revoking stops new use, not what already happened. The 3,280 computer-hours are billed, and whether the cloud company forgives any of it is up to them.
A secrets store moves the risk to whoever may ask it. A computer allowed to read a key can still leak it, so who may ask, and the store's record of who did, matter as much as the store.
Scanning finds what looks like a key, not every secret. A password in a comment or an unusual key can slip past, so scanning backs up the rule of no secrets in code; it doesn't replace it.

Good

rows: Revoke now, new keys in a secrets store
The cost stops at 22:30: 3,280 computer-hours, $4,100.00. No key in code again.
Photo uploads and the pipeline pause until the new keys are in. The bill so far stays.
Commit 41 no longer holds the key on our page.
Copies already taken still hold it, and the key works: 4,480 computer-hours, $5,600.00 by 06:00.
Flags commit 41 at 22:30, and catches the next key. Real practice.
An alert cancels nothing: 4,480 computer-hours, $5,600.00 by 06:00 unless someone revokes.
Strangers can't read the history from now on.
Whoever copied it keeps it, and the key works: $5,600.00 by 06:00.

explain.seniorTake: A secret that reaches a repository should be treated as leaked, and a leaked key as already used. So the order is fixed: revoke it and stop what it started, replace it, check what it touched, and only then tidy the history. Deleting, rewriting and going private all change who can read the code; only revoking changes whether the key works. Then design so it can't happen again: no secrets in code, ever; a secrets store that programs ask at run time, using an identity the cloud gives them; one key per job and per environment, each with only the rights it needs; push protection and secret scanning on every repository; and a spending alert, because the bill is often the first sign.

realWorld.title: FTC, Uber 2016: a key on GitHub, again
realWorld.text: The FTC's business blog on the revised Uber order, April 2018: "Once again, intruders used an access key that an Uber engineer had posted on GitHub."

realWorld.title: FTC: the repository was private
realWorld.text: The same post: "This time, the key was posted to a private GitHub repository." Private did not keep the key safe.

realWorld.title: FTC: what the key opened
realWorld.text: The FTC's press release says Uber learned in November 2016 "that intruders had again accessed consumer data the company stored" "by using an access key an Uber engineer had posted on a code-sharing website."

realWorld.title: GitHub: scanning reads the whole history
realWorld.text: "Secret scanning scans your entire Git history on all branches of your repository for hardcoded credentials"

realWorld.title: GitHub: on an alert, rotate first
realWorld.text: "When you receive an alert, rotate the affected credential immediately to prevent unauthorized access."

realWorld.title: GitHub: rewriting history is the slow part
realWorld.text: "While you can also remove secrets from your Git history, this is time-intensive and often unnecessary if you've already revoked the credential."

realWorld.title: GitHub: push protection
realWorld.text: "Push protection is a secret scanning feature designed to prevent hardcoded credentials, such as secrets or tokens, from ever being pushed to your repository."

realWorld.title: Meli, McNiece and Reaves, NDSS 2019
realWorld.text: "These secrets must be kept private for security, yet common development practices like adding these secrets to code make accidental leakage frequent." They found "that thousands of new, unique secrets are leaked every day."

asked: How do you manage secrets in a service?
A key was pushed to a public repository: what do you do, in order?
Why is rewriting history not enough?
interview.answer: Secrets never go in code or in the repository. The service gets them at run time from a secrets store, proving who it is with an identity the platform gives it, so there is no key to write down. Each service and each environment has its own secrets, with only the rights it needs, and the store records every request, so a leak is small and traceable, and replacing a key means changing it in one place. Push protection blocks commits that hold something shaped like a key, and secret scanning checks the whole history. If a key is pushed to a public repository anyway, treat it as used. First revoke it, and stop anything it started. Second, issue a new key, narrower, into the store. Third, read the provider's use record to see what the leaked key did and clean that up. Last, if you want, rewrite the history, and tell the people affected. Rewriting isn't enough because the repository was never the only copy: anything public has been copied, and the key still works until it is revoked; GitHub itself calls removal from history time-intensive and often unnecessary once the credential is revoked. Making the repository private isn't enough either; in Uber's 2016 breach the key sat in a private repository. A story I'd tell: a flower shop's cloud key was committed and deleted a few minutes later, stayed in a public history for months, and one night started 160 computers; the invoice was for 3,200 computer-hours.

To replace a key with a new one and cancel the old. GitHub's advice on a leaked key is to rotate it immediately.

The site that keeps a team's repositories online, such as GitHub.

The cloud company's list of every request made with a key: when, what it did and where it came from.

A message the cloud company sends when the month's charges pass an amount you set. Eirwen's account had none.

Anything that proves who you are or what you may use, such as a password or a key.

atWork: Search your own repositories' settings, not their code, for one question: is secret scanning on, and is push protection on? Then pick one service and trace where its keys live. It is a common pattern to find a key that was committed and "removed" in the next commit, still valid, still in the history, sometimes with far more rights than its job needs. For each key, check four things. Is it in a secrets store, fetched at run time, or in a file or a commit? Does it belong to one job and one environment, with only the rights that job needs? If it leaked tonight, could you revoke and replace it in minutes, and do you know who would? Is there a spending alert and a use record that someone reads? Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.5.17 (authentication information) expects keys and passwords to be issued, stored and replaced under control, and A.8.4 (access to source code) expects source code and its history to be protected; if SOC 2, criterion CC6.1 covers logical access, including how credentials are kept. Build it in now, with a dated record of where each key lives, what it may do, and when it was last replaced, not at audit time.

recall.prompt: An hour ago a teammate pasted a cloud key into your team's public repository, noticed, and saved a new commit deleting the line. They ask whether that settles it. What do you tell them, and what do you do, in order?

keyIdeas.idea: Revoke the key first, at once: only cancelling it stops its use
The earlier commit still holds the key and copies may already exist, so treat it as compromised
Replace it with a new key kept in a secrets store, not in code

recall.model: No. Deleting the line saved a new commit; the earlier commit still holds the key, and anyone who copied the repository in that hour has it too, so treat it as compromised. First, revoke the key right now, because nothing else stops it working, and stop anything it started. Second, make a new key with only the rights its job needs, and keep it in a secrets store that the program asks at run time, not in code or a settings file. Third, read the provider's use record for anything the old key did. Then turn on push protection and secret scanning, and only if you want it tidy, rewrite the history.

recall.prompt: A key was saved in commit 41 and the line deleted in commit 42 of a public repository. Where can the key still be read?
options: In commit 41, and in any copy of the repository taken before or since
Only on the computer of the person who typed it
Only in the newest version of the file
recall.why: A repository keeps every commit. Deleting a line saves a new commit without it, but commit 41 is unchanged, and every copy of the repository holds it too. Only revoking the key makes what is written there harmless.

recall.prompt: Why give the test copy of a site its own keys instead of the live site's?
options: So a key leaked from the test copy can't reach the live site or its data
The cloud company charges less for test keys
So the test copy can use the live data freely
recall.why: Each environment gets its own secrets, with only the rights it needs. A leak in the test copy, which more people and laptops touch, then stays in the test copy.

recall.prompt: GitHub's secret scanning raises an alert for a cloud key in your repository. What does GitHub advise first?
options: Rewrite the history to remove it
Close the alert as a false alarm
recall.why: GitHub: "When you receive an alert, rotate the affected credential immediately to prevent unauthorized access." Removing it from history is, in GitHub's words, time-intensive and often unnecessary once the credential is revoked.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The cloud company took a share off the bill. Every key now lives in the secrets store, and push protection is on. In February Eirwen hired a student, Pazit, to build a wedding-orders page on a test copy of the site. To save an evening, I pointed the test copy at the same store entry as the live site, so it uses the live photo key. Last week Pazit's laptop was stolen from a café, still signed in to the test copy.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does a stolen test laptop put the live shop at risk, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The test copy reads the live key, so whoever has the laptop can reach the live key; give each environment its own keys
Revoke the live photo key and the laptop's access now, and replace the key
Give the test key only the rights the test copy needs, so a leak there is small

coldCase.model: Because the test copy uses the live key. Whoever holds the laptop, while it is still signed in, can ask the store for the same key the live shop uses, so a test machine is a door into the live shop. Tonight, revoke the live photo key, put a new one in the store, and cut off the test copy's access, signing the laptop out. Then split the environments: the test copy gets its own key, its own storage and test data, and only the rights the test copy needs, so the next stolen laptop reaches nothing that matters. The store's record of requests will show whether anyone used the laptop's access.
